headline: Student Scientists Honor Their Moms by Naming Ancient Frog Species
meta_description: Two interns at Chicago's Field Museum named a newly identified 309-million-year-old amphibian after their mothers, both named Jean.
summary_short: Student scientists Allison Sefcovic and Payton Kohlberg named a newly discovered ancient amphibian after their moms—both called Jean.
body:
When Allison Sefcovic and Payton Kohlberg set out to describe a newly identified frog-like creature that lived 309 million years ago, they decided to honor the two people who supported them most: their mothers. Both women happen to be named Jean, so the young scientists named their discovery *Jeanerpeton mazonensis*—meaning "Jean's crawler from Mazon Creek." The creature, which lived in what is now the swampy area around present-day Chicago, resembled a squat, chubby salamander and represents an early ancestor of today's amphibians. Their findings were published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

What makes the discovery remarkable isn't just the naming story—it's what the fossil reveals about ancient life. The specimen was found years ago by an amateur collector and donated to the Field Museum, where it had been misclassified alongside other poorly understood fossils in what scientists call a "waste bin taxon." Thanks to Sefcovic and Kohlberg's careful study under Dr. Cam So and assistant curator Arjan Mann, *Jeanerpeton* is now recognized as an anatomically distinct species. The fossil preserves extraordinary details: scales on its back, tiny belly ribs called gastralia, and even eye impressions—luxuries of preservation made possible by Mazon Creek's unique conditions as an ancient river delta that quickly buried and fossilized remains.

For the interns, part of the Field Museum's Women in Science program, the project meant more than a publication. Kohlberg reflected on her journey: "Before working in the Mann Lab, I didn't know much about paleontology. My experience has made me more confident in my abilities to try something new." The description of *Jeanerpeton mazonensis* now opens doors for future researchers studying the rich biodiversity that flourished in Mazon Creek millions of years ago—a legacy shaped by two students brave enough to pursue science and thoughtful enough to credit the Jeans behind them.
quick_facts: Two student interns named fossil after both their mothers, Jean
Mazon Creek fossils preserve rare soft tissue details like eye impressions
Specimen had been misclassified for years before study
